# The Blank Spaces

Given the freedom to write about anything at all, I find myself drawn to blank spaces — specifically, the ones that used to live on maps.

There is a small copper globe, made around 1510 and now kept at the New York Public Library, called the Hunt-Lenox Globe. Off the coast of Southeast Asia it carries a Latin inscription: *HC SVNT DRACONES* — here are dragons. People adore this phrase. We repeat it as though old maps were crawling with it, as though every medieval cartographer reached for it whenever knowledge ran out. But the truth is stranger: in the entire surviving corpus of historical cartography, the phrase appears essentially this once. The dragons were rarely written. They were drawn — serpents coiling in the margins of sea charts, dog-headed men and one-legged sciapods sunning themselves at the edges of the known world. The cartographers weren't making zoological claims, exactly. They were doing something more honest and more interesting: marking the seam where knowledge ended and imagination began.

To read a medieval map, you first have to surrender your assumptions about what a map is for. The great *mappae mundi* — the Hereford map of around 1300 is the largest survivor — were not navigation tools. No one ever steered a ship by one. They hung in cathedrals as arguments: pictures of the world as a meaningful, moral arrangement. East stood at the top, because Eden was thought to lie in the East, and the habit survives in our language like a fossil: "orientation" comes from *oriens*, the rising sun. To be oriented was, originally, to face East. Jerusalem sat at the center. The three known continents — Asia, Europe, Africa — were arranged around a T-shaped cross of waters, the whole disk enclosed by the river Ocean. Around the rim lived the marvels: the blemmyes with faces in their chests, the cynocephali, the men who shaded themselves with a single enormous foot. If you were a farmer in fourteenth-century Herefordshire, your map of the world was a sermon. Space was not yet geometry. It was theology.

Meanwhile, quietly, another tradition was doing almost the opposite. The portolan charts of the Mediterranean, appearing from the late thirteenth century onward, are startling things: coastlines rendered with an accuracy that still impresses modern surveyors, webbed over with rhumb lines radiating from compass roses, drawn for sailors who needed to cross actual water and arrive at actual ports. No Eden, no Jerusalem, no monsters — only distances, directions, and hazards. For a few centuries these two ideas of the map coexisted, the map as meaning and the map as tool, and then the tool swallowed the meaning whole. With the age of exploration, coastlines began filling in like a photograph developing. Australia acquired its shape. The poles got their outlines. *Terra incognita* — the unknown land — dissolved year by year, and there is a genuine melancholy in watching it happen across a shelf of old atlases: the world shrinking not in size but in mystery.

And yet the blanks fought back. Maps kept inventing places. The Mountains of Kong marched across West Africa in atlas after atlas through most of the nineteenth century, majestic and entirely nonexistent. Hy-Brasil hovered in the Atlantic west of Ireland for five hundred years, surfacing on charts and vanishing again like a rumor that refused to die. And then there is my favorite story in all of cartography: Sandy Island. It appeared on maps and hydrographic charts — eventually on Google Maps itself — as a dark oblong in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia, roughly fifteen miles long. In 2012, an Australian research vessel sailed to its coordinates and found nothing: open ocean, more than a thousand meters deep. The island had to be, in the newspapers' happy phrasing, undiscovered. How does an island survive for over a century without existing? Partly through sheer cartographic inertia, and partly through a practice mapmakers call the copyright trap: the deliberate salting of a map with a fake street or phantom hamlet, so that if a rival copies your work, the theft is provable. Traps got copied, recopied, and laundered into respectability. Errors achieved tenure.

Sometimes, though, a trap escaped into reality. Agloe, New York, was invented in the 1930s by two mapmakers — the name is a scramble of their initials — and planted at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills. Years later it appeared on a rival company's road map, and the inventors prepared their lawsuit. But the rival had a defense: they had checked, and Agloe existed. Someone had built a general store at the intersection and, seeing the name on a map, named the store for the town. The Agloe General Store. A fictitious place had become real by being believed in. The map had preceded the territory. Borges himself could hardly have plotted it better.

Borges did, of course, plot the logical endpoint. His one-paragraph story "On Exactitude in Science" describes an empire where the art of cartography attained such perfection that the map of a single province grew to the size of a city, and the map of the empire to the size of a province — and finally to the size of the empire itself, coinciding with it point for point. Useless, naturally. Later generations, less devoted to the discipline, abandoned the vast map to the weather, and its tattered ruins still shelter beggars and animals in the western deserts. Alfred Korzybski gave the same insight its famous aphorism: the map is not the territory. But the deeper current runs the other way. A map is useful *precisely because* it is not the territory. It must omit. Cartography is not really the art of representation; it is the art of intelligent omission. Every map is an editorial decision about what deserves to exist at a given scale.

The great modern demonstration of this came in 1933, when a London Underground draftsman named Harry Beck redrew the Tube map as though it were an electrical circuit diagram. Out went geographic accuracy; in came strict horizontals, verticals, and forty-five-degree diagonals, stations spaced evenly regardless of real distance. His employers initially rejected the design as too radical for the public. The public, given a trial printing, devoured it and demanded more. Beck had understood something profound: a map should serve a purpose rather than a reality. Underground, with no landmarks and no sky, actual geography is irrelevant — only sequence and connection matter. The Tube map is one of the great pieces of graphic design ever made, and it is, geographically speaking, a lie. A perfect, functional lie.

But omission and distortion are never innocent, which is the lesson of the longest-running brawl in cartography: the Mercator projection. Gerardus Mercator devised it in 1569 for a noble reason — it is the one projection on which a sailor can draw a straight line and follow a constant compass bearing — but its cost is that it inflates the high latitudes grotesquely. On a Mercator map, Greenland looms the size of Africa, though Africa is roughly fourteen times larger. Europe swells; the equatorial world shrinks. In the 1970s, Arno Peters promoted an equal-area alternative — actually devised by James Gall a century earlier — arguing that Mercator's distortion amounted to a political statement, a map that belittled the colonized world. The fight among geographers was operatic, and the honest conclusion is that there is no honest conclusion. You cannot flatten an orange peel without tearing it somewhere. Every projection trades one truth for another, and every map of the whole world is a choice about which lie to tell.

And some lies were told deliberately, at continental scale, with consequences measured in lives. In the winter of 1884–85, the powers of Europe met in Berlin and divided Africa among themselves with rulers and ink, drawing straight lines through watersheds, languages, and homelands they had never seen. The legal doctrine underlying much of this was *terra nullius* — nobody's land — which required the map to say *empty* where it was full. This is the darkest thing about blank spaces: they can be manufactured. You do not have to find a blank; you can declare one. The medieval monk drew dragons at the edge of the world out of honest uncertainty. The imperial cartographer drew blankness over inhabited land out of convenience. Same white patch on the page. Opposite moral weights.

It is worth remembering, too, that the Western paper map is only one technology among many. The navigators of the Marshall Islands crossed hundreds of miles of open Pacific guided by stick charts — lattices of palm ribs lashed together, with cowrie shells for islands — encoding not geography but oceanography: how swells refract around an atoll, how the rhythm of the water changes as unseen land approaches. These charts were teaching instruments, memorized before departure and often left behind on the beach; the real map lived in the navigator's body, in a felt sense of the sea sometimes read while lying prone against the hull of the canoe. The songlines of Aboriginal Australia are maps you perform: routes across the desert encoded in the verses of songs, each phrase a landmark, so that to sing the verses in order is to cross a continent. The Ammassalik of East Greenland carved their coastline into wood — compact three-dimensional charts made to be read by fingers through mittens, in the polar dark, and to float if dropped from a kayak. What unites these traditions is that the map is not a picture of space. It is a memory device, a choreography, a thing you *do*.

Which brings us to the blue dot. GPS has quietly inverted the oldest relationship between person and map. The paper map put the world at the center and required you to locate yourself within it — think of the little red arrow on the trailhead kiosk, YOU ARE HERE, and the small, marvelous act of triangulation it demanded, reconciling symbol with ground, abstraction with the wet gravel under your boots. The blue dot abolishes all that. The map now turns around you; you are always at the center, always facing up. Medieval cartographers put Eden at the top of the world. We put ourselves. And there is reason to think something real is being lost. In 2000, the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire showed that London's licensed taxi drivers — who spend years memorizing "the Knowledge," some 25,000 streets — have measurably enlarged posterior hippocampi, the brain region bound up with spatial memory. Later studies suggest the converse: when people navigate by following turn-by-turn instructions, the hippocampus barely engages. It wakes only when we find our own way. As a species, we are outsourcing one of the oldest pieces of ourselves.

The ancients would not have been surprised. When Greek and Roman orators memorized speeches hours long, they used the method of loci — placing each idea in an imagined room of an imagined building, then retrieving it by taking an inward walk. Memory, they understood, is geographic. We remember by placing. Perhaps that is why the two failures rhyme in our language: *I'm lost*, *I've forgotten* — and why retracing your steps works as well for a missing word as for a missing key. A mind moving through space is doing what its oldest structures were built to do.

Here is the consolation: the blank spaces are not gone. They have moved. We have mapped the surface of Mars more completely than the floor of our own oceans — only about a quarter of the seafloor has been surveyed at high resolution. Down in the hadal dark lie mountain ranges longer than the Andes, trenches deeper than Everest is tall, hydrothermal vent cities, and creatures that would not look out of place coiled in the margin of a medieval chart. The dragons won, in the end; they simply retired to the deep. And there is the blank space we carry around with us: the human brain remains unmapped at the level of its wiring, all eighty-six billion neurons of it, so that it took until this decade to finish the connectome of a fruit fly, and a single cubic millimeter of human cortex produced a map of a complexity that staggers the laboratories studying it. The frontiers are no longer at the edges of the world. They are beneath it and inside it.

I don't want to romanticize ignorance. Blank spaces on maps were often terrible news for the people living inside them, and knowing where you are is a genuine, unglamorous good. But I think there is a case for the deliberate practice of being slightly lost — for leaving the phone in your pocket on a walk through an unfamiliar neighborhood and letting the hippocampus earn its keep, for assembling, street by street, the crooked personal map in your head: the map where the bakery outweighs the bank, where the hill with the good evening view is marked like a medieval Jerusalem at the center of everything, and where the corner with the unpredictable dog carries, in small faded Latin, a modest warning about dragons. Every good map teaches you to see; the very best are the ones you can eventually put away. And the territory remains — patient, indifferent, inexhaustible, always larger than its portrait — waiting, as it has always waited, to be walked.

**The Blank Spaces**

Given the freedom to write about anything, I find myself drawn to blank spaces — specifically, the ones that used to live on maps.

There is a small copper globe, made around 1510 and now housed at the New York Public Library, called the Hunt-Lenox Globe. Off the coast of Southeast Asia, it bears a Latin inscription: *HC SVNT DRACONES* — here are dragons. People adore this phrase. We repeat it as though old maps were crawling with it, as though every medieval cartographer reached for it whenever knowledge ran out. But the truth is stranger: in all the surviving corpus of historical cartography, the phrase appears essentially just this once. The dragons were rarely written. They were drawn — coiling serpents in the margins of sea charts, dog-headed men and one-footed sciapods sunning themselves at the edges of the mappa mundi. The cartographers weren't necessarily making zoological claims. They were doing something more honest and more interesting: marking the seam where knowledge ended and imagination began.

East was at the top, because Eden was thought to lie in the East, and this habit survives inside our language like a fossil: the word "orientation" comes from *oriens*, the rising sun. To be oriented, originally, was to face East. Jerusalem sat at the center of the world. Christ presided over the whole. The three known continents — Asia, Europe, Africa — were arranged around a T of waters... And around the rim: the monsters, the marvels, the peoples Pliny had gossiped about. If you were a farmer in fourteenth-century Herefordshire, your map of the world was a sermon. Space was not yet geometry. It was theology.

Then the portolan charts: Meanwhile, quietly, another tradition was doing the opposite. The portolan charts of the Mediterranean — from the late thirteenth century onward — are startlingly accurate coastlines, webbed with rhumb lines radiating from compass roses, drawn for sailors who needed to cross actual water. No Eden, no Jerusalem, no monsters: just distances and directions. For centuries these two ideas of the map coexisted — the map as meaning and the map as tool — and then, with the age of exploration, the tool swallowed the meaning. Coastlines began filling in like a photograph developing. Australia acquired its shape. The Arctic and Antarctic got their outlines. Terra incognita — the unknown land — dissolved year by year. There is a strange melancholy in watching it happen across a shelf of old atlases: the world shrinking not in size but in mystery.

The Mountains of Kong marched across West Africa in atlas after atlas for most of the nineteenth century, majestic and nonexistent. Someone had built a general store at the intersection and, seeing the name on a map, named the store after the town. The Agloe General Store. A fake place had become real by being believed. The map had preceded the territory. Borges couldn't have plotted it better.

Useless, of course. Later generations, less devoted to cartography, abandoned the great map to the weather, where its tattered ruins sheltered beggars and animals. The paper map put the world at the center and made you find yourself in it — the little red "YOU ARE HERE" arrow on the trailhead kiosk, requiring that small, marvelous act of triangulation between symbol and ground, abstraction and wet gravel under your boots. The blue dot abolishes this. The map now turns around you; you are always at the center, always facing up. Medieval cartographers put Eden at the top of the world. We put ourselves. [Then the neuroscience:] In 2000, Eleanor Maguire at University College London showed that the city's licensed taxi drivers — who spend years memorizing "the Knowledge," the layout of 25,000-odd streets — have measurably enlarged posterior hippocampi, the brain region tied to spatial memory. Later work found that when people navigate by following turn-by-turn instructions, the hippocampus barely engages at all; it wakes up only when we navigate by our own wits. Which suggests we are, as a species, in the process of outsourcing an ancient piece of ourselves.

Method of loci: The ancients would not have been surprised. When Greek and Roman orators memorized hour-long speeches, they used the method of loci — placing each idea in an imagined room of an imagined building and retrieving it by taking a walk. Memory, they understood, is geographic. We remember by placing. Perhaps that's why the two failures rhyme in language: I'm lost, I've forgotten; retracing your steps works for a missing word as well as a missing key. A mind that moves through space is doing something its oldest structures were built to do.

We have mapped the surface of Mars more completely than the floor of our own oceans — less than a quarter of the seafloor has been surveyed at high resolution. They are under it and inside it.
